prompt.context: Our client is a shrimp restaurant. Currently, a worker shells shrimp manually. The worker needs 15 minutes to set up his workspace for shelling each day. Shelling is not his main task. It takes him 10 minutes to shell one pound of shrimp. His wage is $6 per hour. It is possible to buy a machine for $3,285 that automatically shells shrimp. The machine has a useful life of 3 years. Setup time for the machine is 30 minutes each day. The same worker will operate the machine. The machine can process 60 pounds per hour.
prompt.question: What is the break-even volume of shrimp (in pounds per day) needed to justify the investment in the machine?

clarifying_info.q: How many working days per year should we assume?
Should we assume straight-line depreciation with no salvage value?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, spread the machine cost evenly over its 3-year life.

clarifying_info.q: Does the worker cost anything beyond shelling time (e.g., benefits)?
clarifying_info.a: Use the stated wage of $6 per hour; no other costs.

framework: Calculate daily machine cost by depreciating the purchase price over 3 years (365 days/year)
Calculate variable labor cost per pound under manual shelling
Calculate variable labor cost per pound with the machine
Identify the incremental fixed cost per day from additional setup time
Set up break-even equation: daily machine cost + incremental setup cost = variable cost savings per pound x volume
Solve for break-even pounds per day

questions.prompt: What is the daily cost of the machine?
questions.guidance: Depreciate $3,285 over 3 years x 365 days = 1,095 days. This gives a daily machine cost of $3.

math.setup: Machine cost per day = $3,285 / (3 years x 365 days/year)

questions.prompt: What is the labor cost per pound under manual shelling?
questions.guidance: Worker takes 10 min/pound at $6/hr. Convert: $6/hr = $0.10/min. 10 min x $0.10/min = $1.00/pound.

math.setup: Cost per pound (manual) = (10 min/pound) x ($6/hr / 60 min/hr)

questions.prompt: What is the labor cost per pound with the machine?
questions.guidance: Machine processes 60 lbs/hr. Worker wage is $6/hr. So cost per pound = $6/60 = $0.10/pound.

questions.prompt: What is the incremental daily setup cost from switching to the machine?
questions.guidance: Machine setup is 30 min/day vs. manual setup of 15 min/day. Incremental setup = 15 min/day at $0.10/min = $1.50/day.

questions.prompt: What is the break-even daily volume?
questions.guidance: Total daily fixed cost to recover = machine depreciation + incremental setup = $3 + $1.50 = $4.50. Variable cost saving per pound = $1.00 - $0.10 = $0.90. Break-even volume = $4.50 / $0.90 = 5 pounds per day.

math.setup: Break-even volume = (daily machine cost + incremental setup cost) / variable cost saving per pound

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the pure break-even math, what other factors should the restaurant consider before buying the machine?

categories.name: Volume uncertainty
ideas: Is current daily shrimp usage above or below 5 lbs?
Will volume grow, and by how much?

categories.name: Quality and operations
ideas: Does machine-shelled shrimp meet the restaurant's quality standards?
How does machine reliability/downtime affect service?
What is the maintenance cost of the machine?

categories.name: Financial considerations
ideas: Is $3,285 a significant capital outlay for this restaurant?
What is the opportunity cost of capital?

categories.name: Labor implications
ideas: Does freeing up the worker's manual shelling time create value elsewhere?
Are there any labor contract or HR implications?

categories.name: Risk
ideas: What if the machine breaks down — is a repair/replacement plan in place?
Is the 3-year useful life estimate reliable?

recommendation: If the restaurant shells more than 5 pounds of shrimp per day on a consistent basis, the machine pays for itself and the investment is justified.
Given the low break-even threshold, the machine is likely attractive for any restaurant with non-trivial shrimp usage.
risks: Actual daily volume may be below 5 lbs, especially outside peak periods.
Maintenance and repair costs were not included in the analysis and could raise the effective break-even.
next_steps: Verify actual average daily shrimp volume from purchasing/inventory records.
Obtain a maintenance cost estimate from the machine supplier.
Re-run break-even analysis including maintenance costs before committing to the purchase.
